::: {.callout-note}
## Read this file twice

This document does two jobs at once:

1. **It is the project's instructions.** Rendering it runs the whole analysis, from the raw data to the final figures, in order. If it renders, the project is reproducible.
2. **It is a Quarto tutorial.** Every section introduces the Quarto feature that step needs, in a box like this one.

Open `run-analysis.qmd` (the source) in Positron next to `run-analysis.html` (the rendered output). Everything you see in the HTML was written in the source. The **</> Code** button at the top right of the HTML shows the source too.
:::

# The project at a glance

**Question.** How did life expectancy, fertility, and CO₂ emissions per person change across world regions between 1952 and 2007, and how do they relate to each other?

**Data.** Four public files, combined into one table with one row per country and year:

| File in `data/raw/` | Source | Format | License |
|---|---|---|---|
| `gapminder.tsv` | [Gapminder](https://www.gapminder.org/data/), via the [`gapminder` R package](https://github.com/jennybc/gapminder) | long, tab-separated | CC BY |
| `wb_fertility_wide.csv` | [World Bank WDI](https://data.worldbank.org/indicator/SP.DYN.TFRT.IN), indicator `SP.DYN.TFRT.IN` | **wide**, one column per year | CC BY 4.0 |
| `wb_country_metadata.csv` | Same World Bank download | lookup table: region, income group | CC BY 4.0 |
| `owid_co2_per_capita.csv` | [Our World in Data](https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/co-emissions-per-capita), from the Global Carbon Budget | long | CC BY 4.0 |

More detail on each file is in `data/README.md`.

**Folders.** Every file has one job:

```
266A-example-analysis/
├── run-analysis.qmd        <- this file: render it to run everything
├── README.md               <- points here
├── data/
│   ├── raw/                <- downloaded files, never edited
│   ├── reference/          <- small hand-written lookup tables
│   └── processed/          <- written by the pipeline (not in git)
├── R/                      <- one script per step, plus functions.R
├── python/                 <- the Python step
├── output/
│   ├── figures/            <- written by the pipeline (not in git)
│   └── tables/
├── renv.lock               <- exact R package versions
├── AGENTS.md               <- rules for AI assistants working in this repo
└── STYLE.md                <- code style for humans and AI
```

::: {.callout-tip}
## Quarto: the YAML header

The block between the two `---` lines at the very top of the source is the **YAML header**. It sets options for the whole document:

- `title`, `subtitle`, `author`, `date: today`: the title block you see above.
- `format: html:` and its options: `toc` (table of contents), `number-sections`, `embed-resources: true` (one self-contained `.html` file you can email), `code-tools` (the **</> Code** button).
- `execute:` sets defaults for **every** code chunk. `echo: true` shows the code; `warning: false` hides warnings **and messages** from packages (so helper functions here print with `cat()` instead).

Indentation matters in YAML: two spaces per level, never tabs.
:::

# Before you render (one time only)

You need R, [Quarto](https://quarto.org/docs/get-started/), and Positron. You do **not** need to install Python yourself (see @sec-python).

1. **Get the project.** Clone the repository, then in Positron use *File → Open Folder* and choose `266A-example-analysis`. Opening the folder makes it the working directory, so every path in this project can be relative.

2. **Install the exact package versions.** This project uses [`renv`](https://rstudio.github.io/renv/). When you open the folder, `renv` starts automatically (via `.Rprofile`). In the R console, run:

```{r}
#| label: restore
#| eval: false
renv::restore()
```

This reads `renv.lock` and installs the same versions of every package that were used to produce these results, in a library that belongs to this project only.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Quarto: code chunks and chunk options

A code chunk starts with ```` ```{r} ```` and ends with ```` ``` ````. Lines at the top that start with `#|` are **chunk options**:

- `label: restore` names the chunk. Labels show up in error messages, so you know where a render failed.
- `eval: false` shows the code **without running it**. We want you to run `renv::restore()` yourself, once, not every time the document renders.

Other options you will see below: `include: false` (run it but show nothing), `echo: false` (show the output, hide the code), and `fig-cap` (a figure caption).
:::

# Step 0: setup

```{r}
#| label: setup
source("R/functions.R")
```

This loads the helper functions every step uses: `check_unique_key()` stops the render if a table has duplicated keys, and `report_rows()` prints row counts so changes are visible.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Quarto: everything runs in order, in a fresh session

When you render, Quarto starts a **new R session** and runs every chunk from top to bottom. Nothing from your console exists there: a data frame you created by hand, a package you loaded interactively, a variable you changed. If the analysis needs it, a chunk must create it.

This is what makes the document a test of reproducibility. *"It works on my machine"* is not enough; it has to work in a fresh session.
:::

# Step 1: import

```{r}
#| label: import
source("R/01-import.R")
```

This reads the four raw files in `data/raw/` without changing them (see the comments in `R/01-import.R` for what each `read_*()` option is for). The Gapminder file has `r nrow(gapminder_raw)` rows covering `r length(unique(gapminder_raw$country))` countries; the World Bank file has `r nrow(fertility_raw)` rows, because it mixes countries with groups of countries such as "World".

::: {.callout-tip}
## Quarto: inline code

The numbers in the paragraph above were not typed. In the source they are written as `` `r knitr::inline_expr("nrow(gapminder_raw)")` ``, which runs when you render and inserts the result into the text. If the data change, the sentence changes with them. Use inline code for every number you report in a sentence.
:::

A quick look at the wide World Bank table, which is the one that needs reshaping:

```{r}
#| label: peek-wide
fertility_raw[1:3, 1:8]
```

# Step 2: clean

```{r}
#| label: clean
source("R/02-clean.R")
```

The main job here is to give every country the **same key** in every table. Gapminder identifies countries by name, the other files by ISO3 code (`"MEX"`, `"KEN"`, ...). We take each name's code from the OWID file. Eleven Gapminder names are spelled differently there, so they get their codes from a small hand-written table, @tbl-fixes.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-fixes
#| tbl-cap: "Gapminder country names that do not match the OWID file, from data/reference/country_name_fixes.csv."
knitr::kable(name_fixes)
```

::: {.callout-tip}
## Quarto: tables and cross-references

The chunk above has `label: tbl-fixes` and a `tbl-cap`. Because the label starts with `tbl-`, Quarto numbers the table and lets you refer to it as `@tbl-fixes` in the text, which becomes the clickable "Table 1" you saw. Figures work the same way with the `fig-` prefix, and sections with `{#sec-...}`.

Why a CSV and not code? The lookup is *data*. Keeping it in `data/reference/` means fixing a new mismatch is a one-line edit that anyone can review.
:::

::: {.callout-warning}
## A step that stops the render on purpose

`R/02-clean.R` contains `stopifnot(!any(is.na(gapminder$iso3)))`. If a country name ever fails to match, the render **stops with an error** instead of quietly dropping that country. A render that fails loudly is better than a report that is quietly wrong.
:::

# Step 3: reshape and join

```{r}
#| label: reshape-join
source("R/03-reshape-join.R")
```

The World Bank file is reshaped from wide (one column per year) to long (one row per country-year) with `pivot_longer()`, then the four sources are joined on `iso3` and `year`. Gapminder decides which rows we keep; the others only add columns.

The final analysis table has `r nrow(analysis)` rows, `r length(unique(analysis$country))` countries, and covers `r min(analysis$year)` to `r max(analysis$year)`. It is saved as `data/processed/analysis.csv`.

```{r}
#| label: peek-analysis
head(analysis)
```

# Step 4: a Python step {#sec-python}

```{r}
#| label: python-setup
#| message: false
library(reticulate)
py_require("pandas>=2.2")
```

The next chunk is **Python**, not R. It receives the R data frame `analysis`, computes the correlation between fertility and life expectancy within each region, and hands the result back to R.

```{python}
#| label: py-correlations
import sys
sys.path.insert(0, "python")
from summarize import regionCorrelations

correlations = regionCorrelations(r.analysis, 2007)
correlations
```

Back in R, the Python result is available as `py$correlations`:

```{r}
#| label: tbl-correlations
#| tbl-cap: "Correlation between fertility and life expectancy across countries within each region, 2007 (computed in Python)."
knitr::kable(py$correlations, digits = 2, row.names = FALSE)
```

In most regions, countries with higher fertility have lower life expectancy (@tbl-correlations). Europe & Central Asia is the exception: fertility there is low almost everywhere, so it says little about life expectancy. Read the `n_countries` column too: a correlation of −1 from two North American countries means nothing.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Quarto: mixing R and Python in one document

- A chunk that starts with ```` ```{python} ```` runs Python. Because this document also has R chunks, Quarto uses the **knitr** engine and runs the Python chunks through the R package **reticulate**. Both languages share one session.
- **R → Python:** inside a Python chunk, `r.analysis` is the R object `analysis`, converted to a pandas DataFrame.
- **Python → R:** inside an R chunk, `py$correlations` is the Python object `correlations`, converted to an R data frame.
- `py_require("pandas>=2.2")` declares which Python packages this document needs. The first time you render, reticulate downloads Python and pandas into a cache, so nobody has to install Python by hand. (You need an internet connection the first time.)
- Longer Python code lives in `python/summarize.py`, just as longer R code lives in `R/`. The chunk only imports it and calls it.
:::

# Step 5: describe

```{r}
#| label: describe
source("R/04-describe.R")
```

This writes a summary table to `output/tables/region_summary.csv` and two figures to `output/figures/`.

```{r}
#| label: fig-scatter
#| fig-cap: "Fertility and life expectancy in 2007. Each point is a country; size is population."
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 5
fig_scatter
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-trends
#| fig-cap: "Median of each variable across the countries in each World Bank region."
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 8
fig_trends
```

@fig-scatter shows a strong negative relationship in 2007: where women have fewer children, people live longer. @fig-trends shows that the median fertility fell and the median life expectancy rose in every region. CO₂ per person rose everywhere too, but stayed far higher in North America and Europe than in South Asia and Sub-Saharan Africa. These are descriptions, not causes: all three variables move with income and time.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Quarto: figures

A chunk whose label starts with `fig-` and has a `fig-cap` becomes a numbered figure you can cite with `@fig-scatter`. `fig-width` and `fig-height` (in inches) control its size. The same figures are also saved as PNG files by `R/04-describe.R`, so you can use them in slides without re-running anything.
:::

# How to render, and how to check it is reproducible

**Render** in one of two ways:

- In Positron: open `run-analysis.qmd` and click **Preview** (or press `Ctrl/Cmd + Shift + K`).
- In the terminal, from the project folder:

```bash
quarto render run-analysis.qmd
```

**Check it is reproducible.** The real test is a fresh start:

1. Delete everything the pipeline creates: the files in `data/processed/` and `output/` (keep the `.gitkeep` files).
2. Restart R (*Session → Restart R*), so nothing is left in memory.
3. Render again. Every file comes back, and the numbers in this document stay the same.

The best test of all: clone the repository into a new folder (or a classmate's laptop) and render there.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Quarto: where code runs from

Code chunks run with the **project folder** as the working directory (set in `_quarto.yml` with `execute-dir: project`). That is why every path in this project is relative, like `"data/raw/gapminder.tsv"`. A path like `"/Users/marce/Desktop/..."` works only on one laptop, and breaks the first time anyone else renders.

For long analyses, Quarto can also skip chunks that have not changed (`freeze` and `cache` options). This project is small enough to re-run in full every time, which is the safest choice.
:::
